stem: A trust deed specifies a perpetuity-due: payments of Rs 7,000 are made at the beginning of each year forever. If the annual discount rate is 5%, what is the present value of this perpetuity-due?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Uses ordinary perpetuity PV = C / r = 7000 / 0.05 = 1,40,000, ignoring that payments start at the beginning of each period.
Divides 7000 by 0.0525 (uses a quarter-adjusted rate of 5.25%) giving approximately 1,33,333.
Computes 1,40,000 * 1.05 but drops the last digit, arriving at 1,34,000 instead of 1,47,000.

explanation: A perpetuity-due pays at the start of each period, so every payment is one period earlier than in an ordinary perpetuity. The PV is therefore (1+r) times the ordinary perpetuity PV.

explanation_sections.punchline: Perpetuity-due PV = (C / r) * (1 + r): the timing shift from end-of-period to beginning-of-period multiplies the ordinary PV by (1+r).
explanation_sections.approach: Name the formula PV-due = (C/r)*(1+r). Map: C = 7000, r = 0.05. Compute ordinary PV = 7000 / 0.05 = 1,40,000. Scale up: 1,40,000 * 1.05 = 1,47,000.
explanation_sections.lesson: Perpetuity-due and ordinary perpetuity differ by a factor of (1+r). Always check whether the question specifies beginning or end of period.
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. The most common trap is stopping at 1,40,000. If you see that option it is the ordinary-perpetuity answer.
